elements.id-string-13: Existing research on \textit{task incremental learning} in continual learning has primarily focused on preventing \textit{catastrophic forgetting} (CF).Although several techniques have achieved learning with no CF, they attain it by letting each task monopolize a sub-network in a shared network, which seriously limits knowledge transfer (KT) and causes over-consumption of the network capacity, i.e., as more tasks are learned, the performance deteriorates.The goal of this paper is threefold: (1) overcoming CF, (2) encouraging KT, and (3) tackling the capacity problem.A novel technique (called SPG) is proposed that \textit{soft-masks} (partially blocks) parameter updating in training based on the importance of each parameter to old tasks.Each task still uses the full network, i.e., no monopoly of any part of the network by any task, which enables maximum KT and reduction in capacity usage.To our knowledge, this is the first work that soft-masks a model at the parameter-level for continual learning.Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SPG in achieving all three objectives.More notably, it attains significant transfer of knowledge not only among similar tasks (with shared knowledge) but also among dissimilar tasks (with little shared knowledge) while mitigating CF.
elements.id-string-15: Catastrophic forgetting (CF) and knowledge transfer (KT) are two key challenges of continual learning (CL), which learns a sequence of tasks incrementally.
elements.id-string-16: CF refers to the phenomenon where a model loses some of its performance on previous tasks once it learns a new task.
elements.id-string-17: KT means that tasks may help each other to learn by sharing knowledge.
elements.id-string-18: This work further investigates these problems in the popular CL paradigm, \textit{task-incremental learning} (TIL).
elements.id-string-19: In TIL, each task consists of several classes of objects to be learned.
elements.id-string-20: Once a task is learned, its data is discarded and will not be available for later use.
elements.id-string-21: During testing, the task id is provided for each test sample so that the corresponding classification head of the task can be used for prediction.
elements.id-string-22: Several effective approaches have been proposed for TIL that can achieve learning with little or no CF.
elements.id-string-23: \textit{Parameter isolation} is perhaps the most successful one in which the system learns to mask a sub-network for each task in a shared network.
elements.id-string-24: HAT~\citep{hat} and SupSup~\citep{supsup} are two representative systems.
elements.id-string-25: HAT set binary/hard masks on neurons (not parameters) that are important for each task.
elements.id-string-26: In learning a new task, those masks block the gradient flow through the masked neurons in the backward pass.
elements.id-string-27: Only those \textit{free} (unmasked) \textit{neurons} and their parameters are trainable.
elements.id-string-28: Thus, as more tasks are learned, the number of free neurons left becomes fewer, making later tasks harder to learn, which results in gradual performance deterioration (see \cref{sec:capacity}).
elements.id-string-29: Further, if a neuron is masked, all the parameters feeding to it are also masked, which consumes \textbf{a great deal of network capacity} (hereafter referred to as the ``capacity problem'').
elements.id-string-30: As the sub-networks for old tasks cannot be updated, it has \textbf{limited knowledge transfer}.
elements.id-string-31: CAT~\citep{cat} tries to improve KT of HAT by detecting task similarities.
elements.id-string-32: If the new task is found similar to some previous tasks, these tasks' masks are removed so that the new task training can update the parameters of these tasks for backward pass.
elements.id-string-33: However, this is risky because if a dissimilar task is detected as similar, serious CF occurs, and if similar tasks are detected as dissimilar, its knowledge transfer will be limited.
elements.id-string-34: SupSup uses a backbone network (randomly initialized) and finds a sub-network for each task.
elements.id-string-35: The sub-network is represented by a mask, which is a set of binary gates indicating which parameters in the network are used.
elements.id-string-36: The mask for each task is saved.
elements.id-string-37: Since the network is not changed, SupSup has no CF or capacity problem, but since each mask is independent of other masks, SupSup by design has no KT.
elements.id-string-38: To tackle these problems, we propose a very different approach, named ``\underline{\textit{S}}oft-masking of \underline{\textit{P}}arameter-level \underline{\textit{G}}radient flow'' (SPG).
elements.id-string-39: It is surprisingly effective and contributes in following ways:
elements.id-string-40: (1).~Instead of learning hard/binary masks on neurons for each task and blocking these neurons in training a new task and in testing like HAT, SPG computes an importance score for each network parameter (not neuron) to old tasks using gradients.
elements.id-string-41: The reason that gradients can be used as importance is because gradients directly tell how a change to a specific parameter will affect the output classification and may cause CF.
elements.id-string-42: SPG uses the importance score of each parameter as a \textit{soft-mask} to constrain the gradient flow in the backward pass to ensure those important parameters to old tasks have minimum changes in learning a new task to prevent CF of previous knowledge.
elements.id-string-43: To our knowledge, soft-masking of parameters has not been done before.
elements.id-string-44: (2).~SPG has some resemblance to the popular regularization-based approach, e.g., EWC~\citep{ewc}, in that both use importance of parameters to constrain changes to important parameters of old tasks.
elements.id-string-45: But there is a major difference.
elements.id-string-46: SPG directly controls each parameter (fine-grained), but EWC controls all parameters together using a regularization term in the loss to penalize the sum of changes to all parameters in the network (rather coarse-grained).
elements.id-string-47: \cref{sec:results} shows that our \textbf{soft-masking is markedly better than regularization}.
elements.id-string-48: We believe this is an important result.
elements.id-string-49: (3).~In the forward pass, no masks are applied, which encourages knowledge transfer among tasks.
elements.id-string-50: This is better than CAT as SPG does not need extra mechanism for task similarity comparison.
elements.id-string-51: Knowledge sharing and transfer in SPG are automatic.
elements.id-string-53: (4).~As SPG soft-masks parameters, it does not monopolize any parameters or sub-network like HAT for each task and SPG's forward pass does not use any masks.
elements.id-string-55: Experiments with the standard CL setup have been conducted with (1) similar tasks to demonstrate SPG's better knowledge transfer
elements.id-string-56: and (2) dissimilar tasks to show SPG's ability to overcome CF, and (3) deal with the capacity issue.
elements.id-string-57: None of the baselines is able to achieve all.
elements.id-string-60: Approaches in continual learning can be grouped into three main categories.
elements.id-string-63: This approach computes importance values of either parameters or their gradients on previous tasks, and adds a regularization in the loss to restrict changes to those important parameters to mitigate CF.
elements.id-string-64: EWC~\citep{ewc} uses the Fisher information matrix to represent the importance of parameters and a regularization to penalize the sum of changes to all parameters.
elements.id-string-65: SI~\citep{si} extends EWC to reduce the complexity in computing the penalty.
elements.id-string-66: Many other approaches~\citep{lwf,dmc,ucl} in this category have also been proposed, but they still have difficulty to prevent CF.
elements.id-string-67: As discussed in the introduction section, the proposed approach SPG has some resemblance to a  regularization based method EWC.
elements.id-string-68: But the coarse-grained approach of using regularization is significant poorer than the fine-grained soft-masking in SPG for overcoming CF as we will see in \cref{sec:results}.
elements.id-string-70: This approach introduces a small memory buffer to store data of previous tasks and replay them in learning a new task to prevent CF~\citep{gem,a-gem}.
elements.id-string-71: Some methods~\citep{gr,binplay} prepare data generators for previous tasks, and the generated pseudo-samples are used instead of real samples.
elements.id-string-72: Although several other approaches~\citep{icarl,mer,mir} have been proposed, they still suffer from CF.
elements.id-string-73: SPG does not save replay data or generate pseudo-replay data.
elements.id-string-75: This approach is most similar to ours SPG.
elements.id-string-76: It tries to learn a sub-network for each task (tasks may share parameters and neurons), which limits knowledge transfer.
elements.id-string-77: We have discussed HAT, SupSup, and CAT in \cref{sec:introduction}.
elements.id-string-78: Many others also take similar approaches, e.g.,
elements.id-string-79: Progressive Networks (PGN)~\citep{pgn}, APD~\citep{apd}, PathNet~\citep{pathnet}, PackNet~\citep{packnet}, SpaceNet~\citep{spacenet}, and WSN~\citep{wsn}.
elements.id-string-80: In particular, PGN allocates a sub-network for each task in advance, and progressively concatenates previous sub-networks while freezing parameters allocated to previous tasks.
elements.id-string-81: APD selectively reuses and dynamically expands the dense network.
elements.id-string-82: Those methods, however, depend on the expansion of network for their performance, which is often not acceptable in cases where many tasks need to be learned.
elements.id-string-83: PathNet splits each layer into multiple sub-modules and finds the best \textit{pathway} designated to each task.
elements.id-string-84: PackNet freezes important weights for each task by finding them based on pruning.
elements.id-string-85: Although PathNet and PackNet do not expand
elements.id-string-86: the network along with continual learning, they suffer from  over-consumption of the fixed capacity.
elements.id-string-87: To address this, SpaceNet adopts the sparse training to preserve parameters for future tasks but the performance for each task is sacrificed.
elements.id-string-88: WSN also allocates a subnetwork within a dense network
elements.id-string-89: and selectively reuses subnetworks for previous tasks without expanding the whole network.
elements.id-string-90: Nevertheless, those methods are still limited by the pre-allocated network size as each task monopolizes and consumes some amount of capacity, which results in poorer KT when learning many tasks.
elements.id-string-91: In summary, parameter isolation-based methods suffer from over-consumption of network capacity and have limited KT, which the proposed method tries to address at the same time.

Black (solid) and green (dashed) arrows represent forward and backward propagation, respectively. $H_t$ denotes the head for task $t$. \textbf{(a)} Training of a model. In the forward pass, nothing extra is done. In the backward pass, the gradients of parameters in the feature extractor $\bm{g}_i$ are changed to $\bm{g}'_i$, based on the accumulated importance ($\bm{\gamma}_i^{\le t-1}$). For parameters of the head for task $t$, their gradients $\bm{g}_{H_t}$ are changed to $\bm{g}'_{H_t}$ using the average of accumulated importance ($\bar{\bm{\gamma}}^{\le t-1}$). \textbf{(b)} Computation of the accumulated importance $\bm{\gamma}_i^{\le t}$. }  \end{figure}
elements.id-string-94: As discussed in \cref{sec:introduction}, the current parameter isolation approaches like HAT~\citep{hat} and SupSup~\citep{supsup} are very effective for overcoming CF, but they hinder knowledge transfer and/or consume too much learning capacity of the network.
elements.id-string-95: For such a model to improve knowledge transfer, it needs to decide which parameters can be shared and updated for a new task.
elements.id-string-96: That is the approach taken in CAT~\citep{cat}.
elements.id-string-97: CAT  finds similar tasks and removes their masks for updating, but may find wrong similar tasks, which causes CF.
elements.id-string-98: Further, parameters are the atomic information units, not neurons, which HAT masks.
elements.id-string-99: If a neuron is masked, all parameters feeding into it are masked, which costs a huge amount of learning capacity.
elements.id-string-100: SPG directly soft-masks parameters based on their importance to previous tasks, which is a more flexible and uses much less learning space.
elements.id-string-101: Soft-masking clearly enables automatic knowledge transfer.

elements.id-string-109: In SPG, the importance of a parameter to a task is computed based on its gradient.
elements.id-string-110: We do so because gradients of parameters directly and quantitatively reflect how much changing a parameter affects the final loss.
elements.id-string-111: Additionally, we normalize the gradients of the parameters within each layer to make relative importance more reliable as gradients in different layers can have different magnitude.
elements.id-string-112: The normalized importance scores are accumulated by which the corresponding gradients are reduced in the optimization step to avoid forgetting the knowledge learned from the previous tasks.
elements.id-string-115: The importance of each parameter to task $t$ is computed right after completing the training of task $t$ following these steps.
elements.id-string-116: Task $t$'s training data, $(\bm{X}_t, \bm{Y}_t)$, is given again to the trained model of task $t$, and the gradient of each parameter in $i$-th layer (i.e., each weight or bias of each layer) is then computed and used for computing the importance of the parameter.
elements.id-string-117: Note that we use $\bm{\theta}_i$ (a vector) to represent all parameters of the $i$-th layer.
elements.id-string-118: This process does not update the model parameters.
elements.id-string-119: The reason that the importance is computed after training of the current task has converged is as follows.
elements.id-string-120: Even after a model converges, some parameters can have larger gradients, which indicate that changing those parameters may take the model out of the (local) minimum leading to forgetting.
elements.id-string-121: On the contrary, if all parameters have similar gradients (i.e, balanced directions of gradients), changing the parameters will not likely to change the model much to cause forgetting.
elements.id-string-122: Based on this assumption, we utilize the normalized gradients after training as a signal to indicate such dangerous parameter updates.
elements.id-string-123: The proposed mechanism in SPG has the merit that it keeps the model flexible as it does not fully block parameters using an importance threshold or binary masks.
elements.id-string-124: While HAT completely blocks important neurons, which results in the loss of trainable parameters over time, SPG allows most parameters remain ``alive'' even when most of them do not change much.

In the above figures, ${}^th_i^l$ and $w_{ij}^l$ represents the output of the $i$-th neuron in the $l$-th layer just after training task $t$ and the parameter in $l$-th layer connecting between the neurons ${}^th_i^l$ to ${}^th_j^{l+1}$, respectively. \textbf{(a)} The importance of $w_{ij}^l$ to task $\tau$ is computed based on its gradient, ${\partial \mathcal{L}^{\tau,\tau}}/{\partial w_{ij}^{l}}$ and then accumulated. \textbf{(b)} After learning task $t$ ($t > \tau$), the state of related parameters might have been changed. elements.id-string-330: As SPG has three core mechanisms that contribute to its performance, we evaluate whether each of them is beneficial.
elements.id-string-331: The first one is \textit{\underline{c}ross-\underline{h}ead \underline{i}mportance} (CHI), which is introduced in \cref{eq:gamma_i_t} with the motivation of suppressing the update of important parameters for previous tasks more.
elements.id-string-332: In the ablation \textbf{SPG (w/o CHI)}, $\bm{\gamma}_i^t$ is replaced with $\bm{\gamma}_i^{t,t}$ in \cref{eq:gamma_i_t} and the previous tasks' heads are not used for computing importance.
elements.id-string-333: The second one is \underline{\textit{s}}oft-\underline{\textit{m}}asking of each \underline{\textit{h}}ead (SMH), which is introduced in \cref{eq:g_ht_prime} for the purpose of balancing the training of the feature extractor and the classification head.
elements.id-string-334: In the ablation \textbf{SPG (w/o SMH)}, \cref{eq:g_ht_prime} is not employed.
elements.id-string-335: The last one is soft-masking (not hard-masking), which is the core technique of SPG to keep most parameters trainable while mitigating CF.
elements.id-string-336: While the reported results so far are based on soft-masking, it is also possible to convert the importance to binary (0 or 1) masks using a pre-defined threshold.
elements.id-string-337: In the ablation \textbf{SPG (w/ hard-masking)}, if the threshold is 0.6, this variant treats importance larger than 0.6 as 1 (blocking updates of parameters), otherwise 0 (not blocking).
elements.id-string-338: We search for the best threshold for each dataset from $\{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\}$.
elements.id-string-339: The ablation results are presented in \cref{tab:results_ablation}.
elements.id-string-340: For CHI, it improves the performance especially in dissimilar tasks (up to 5.5\% for C-20) by blocking more gradient flow to mitigate CF.
elements.id-string-341: On the other hand, CHI does not contributes much for similar tasks, which is reasonable as blocking parameters becomes less important in similar tasks.
elements.id-string-343: SPG with CHI still works the best for similar tasks on average and CHI does not cause side effects.
elements.id-string-344: More quantitative analysis of how CHI contributes to suppressing parameter updates is given in \cref{sec:app_chi}.
elements.id-string-345: For SMH, it delivers positive performance gains both in dissimilar and similar tasks.
elements.id-string-346: These results indicate that the lack of balance in the training between the feature extractor and head, which can happen without SMH, adversely affects the performance.
elements.id-string-347: The promotion of knowledge transfer by SMH becomes most prominent for I-100 (up to 2.9\%) as the effectiveness of knowledge transfer is more important in such an extreme case with more tasks.
elements.id-string-348: For whether masking should be soft or hard, SPG with hard-masking is significantly worse than SPG with soft-masking, which demonstrates that it is difficult to find a good threshold for hard-masking.
elements.id-string-349: Soft-masking is more flexible and effective.
elements.id-string-350: These results clearly confirm that SPG enjoys all of the three different mechanisms.
elements.id-string-352: To overcome the difficulty of balancing forgetting prevention and knowledge transfer in continual learning, we proposed a novel and simple method, called SPG, that blocks/masks parameters not completely but partially to give the model more flexibility and capacity to learn.
elements.id-string-353: The proposed soft-masking mechanism not only overcomes CF but also performs knowledge transfer automatically.
elements.id-string-354: Although it is conceptually related to the regularization approach, as we have argued and evaluated, it markedly outperforms the regularization approach.
elements.id-string-355: Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPG markedly outperforms all the strong baselines.

elements.id-string-385: As we described in \cref{sec:capacity}, SPG blocks much fewer parameters than what HAT does in all cases.
elements.id-string-386: Additionally, we can see from \cref{tab:app_blocking_ratio_layerwise} the significant difference between HAT and SPG in their layer-wise tendency.
elements.id-string-387: HAT blocks more parameters in earlier layers (e.g., after learning task 5 of C-10, 77.8\% of parameters in the 1st convolution layer are completely blocked while 52.4\% of the ones in the 2nd convolution layer are), which is reasonable given that the earlier layers are supposed to extract basic features and thus changing their parameters without being blocked could easily cause more forgetting than in later layers.
elements.id-string-388: On the other hand, SPG contrarily tends to completely block more parameters in later layers (e.g., after learning task 5 of C-10, 0.0\% of parameters in the 1st convolution layer are completely blocked while 0.6\% of ones in 2nd convolution layer are).
elements.id-string-389: Since SPG computes parameters' importance based on their gradients with regard to the loss through normalization, this result implies that later layers are likely to have more parameters on which some of the tasks highly depend.
elements.id-string-390: It can be said that SPG keeps earlier layers alive with less blocking for better basic feature learning (i.e., leading to positive knowledge transfer) while it blocks some specific parameters in later layers that are supposed to be important for previous tasks, which is different from what HAT does.
elements.id-string-392: We analyze in detail how CHI quantitatively contributes to suppressing parameter updates with the following four metrics.
elements.id-string-394: How often does the importance from CHI have a larger value than the one from the current task (1 means that it always happens)?
elements.id-string-395: It corresponds to cases where $\bm{\gamma}_i^{t,\tau} > \bm{\gamma}_i^{t,t}$ for any $\tau (1 \le \tau < t)$ in \cref{eq:gamma_i_t}.
elements.id-string-397: When the cases of F-each happen, how much is the difference of overwriting on average?
elements.id-string-398: It is defined by the average of $\max{(\bm{\gamma}_i^{t,1},\cdots,\bm{\gamma}_i^{t,t-1})} - \bm{\gamma}_i^{t,t}$.
elements.id-string-400: How often does the importance from CHI actually overwrite the accumulated importance through the maximum operation?
elements.id-string-401: It corresponds to cases where $\bm{\gamma}_i^{t,\tau} > \bm{\gamma}_i^{\le t-1}$ for any $\tau (1 \le \tau < t)$ in \cref{eq:gamma_i_le_t}.
elements.id-string-403: When the cases of F-total happen, how much is the difference of overwriting on average?
elements.id-string-404: It is defined by the average of $\max{(\bm{\gamma}_i^{t,1},\cdots,\bm{\gamma}_i^{t,t-1})} - \bm{\gamma}_i^{\le t-1}$.
elements.id-string-406: We can clearly observe that CHI adds more importance to some parameters (e.g., in C-10, about 15-42\% of parameters constantly update their accumulated importance by the ones from CHI), which is denoted by F-total.
elements.id-string-407: Since we introduce CHI to further mitigate forgetting by accumulating more importance, this expectation is consistent with the observed results.
elements.id-string-408: Although CHI also overwrites the accumulated importance in similar tasks as frequently as in dissimilar tasks (see F-each and F-total), it happens with a smaller gap overall (see G-each and G-total), which is reasonable as the tasks are similar thus parameters can have similar gradients among different tasks.
